theory.intro: When the top of a fraction is the derivative of the bottom, the primitive is a logarithm: $\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)| + C$. Always check the numerator first, because without $f'(x)$ the rule does not apply.
facts: The denominator is $f(x)$, and it must appear to the power $1$ for this rule to work.
Differentiate the denominator and compare it with the numerator before choosing this rule.
A constant multiple is enough: if the numerator is $kf'(x)$, the answer is $k\ln|f(x)| + C$.
For $\int\dfrac{x}{x^{2}+7}\,dx$ you need $2x$ on top, so the answer is $\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|x^{2}+7| + C$.
The rule fails when the numerator is not a constant multiple of $f'(x)$, as in $\int\dfrac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1}\,dx$.
A squared denominator needs the reverse chain rule for powers, not this logarithm rule.
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$, writing $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ gives $\int\tan x\,dx = -\ln|\cos x| + C$.
Where $f(x)$ is always positive, such as $e^{x}+1$, the modulus signs may be dropped.
Check any answer by differentiating it with the chain rule.
steps: Identify $f(x)$ as the denominator, which must have power $1$.
Differentiate $f(x)$ and check the numerator is $f'(x)$ or a constant multiple of it.
Adjust for any missing constant factor.
Write the answer as $k\ln|f(x)| + C$ when the numerator is $kf'(x)$, retaining the constant adjustment from step 3.

workedExamples.solution_text:
The denominator is $f(x)=3x^{2}+5x-8$, with derivative $f'(x)=6x+5$. The numerator matches exactly.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{6x+5}{3x^{2}+5x-8}\,dx\\&=\ln|3x^{2}+5x-8|+C\end{aligned}$
This primitive applies on any interval where $3x^{2}+5x-8\ne0$.

For $f(x)=16-x^{2}$, we need $f'(x)=-2x$. Since $3x=-\dfrac{3}{2}(-2x)$, take the constant adjustment outside the integral.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{3x}{16-x^{2}}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\int\dfrac{-2x}{16-x^{2}}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\ln|16-x^{2}|+C\end{aligned}$

For $f(x)=e^{4x}+7$, we need $f'(x)=4e^{4x}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{e^{4x}}{e^{4x}+7}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}\int\dfrac{4e^{4x}}{e^{4x}+7}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln(e^{4x}+7)+C\end{aligned}$
The denominator is positive for every real $x$, so modulus signs are unnecessary.

workedExamples.question_text:
Find:
a. $\int\dfrac{\cos x}{6+3\sin x}\,dx$
b. $\int\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{4+\tan x}\,dx$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. For $f(x)=6+3\sin x$, we need $f'(x)=3\cos x$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{\cos x}{6+3\sin x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{3\cos x}{6+3\sin x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln(6+3\sin x)+C\end{aligned}$
Here $6+3\sin x\ge3$, so the denominator is positive.

b. For $f(x)=4+\tan x$, its derivative $f'(x)=\sec^{2}x$ matches the numerator.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{4+\tan x}\,dx\\&=\ln|4+\tan x|+C\end{aligned}$
This applies on intervals where $\tan x$ is defined and $4+\tan x\ne0$.

workedExamples.question_text: Use $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to evaluate $\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\tan x\,dx$ exactly.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The denominator is $f(x)=\cos x$, with derivative $f'(x)=-\sin x$. The numerator needs a factor of $-1$. Also, $\cos x>0$ throughout $[0,\pi/3]$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\tan x\,dx\\&=\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx\\&=-\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx\\&=\left[-\ln|\cos x|\right]_{0}^{\pi/3}\\&=-\ln\dfrac{1}{2}+\ln1\\&=\ln2\end{aligned}$

For $f(x)=x^{2}+8$, we need $f'(x)=2x$. The denominator is positive throughout the interval.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{3x}{x^{2}+8}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}+8}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}\left[\ln(x^{2}+8)\right]_{1}^{2}\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}(\ln12-\ln9)\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{3}\\&=\ln\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{3/2}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\ln(3x))\\&=\dfrac{1}{\ln(3x)}\times\dfrac{3}{3x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{x\ln(3x)}\end{aligned}$
The integrand is exactly this derivative. Since $x>\dfrac{1}{3}$, we have $\ln(3x)>0$.
$\int\dfrac{1}{x\ln(3x)}\,dx=\ln(\ln(3x))+C$

workedExamples.question_text: A curve has gradient $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{8x}{4x^{2}+3}$ and passes through $(0,2)$. Find its equation.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The derivative of $4x^{2}+3$ is $8x$, matching the numerator.
$y=\ln(4x^{2}+3)+C$
Using $(0,2)$:
$\begin{aligned}\ln3+C&=2\\C&=2-\ln3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln(4x^{2}+3)+2-\ln3\\y&=\ln\dfrac{4x^{2}+3}{3}+2\end{aligned}$

The denominator is zero at $x=2$, which lies inside $[0,3]$. The integrand has a vertical asymptote there.
Although $2x$ is the derivative of $x^{2}-4$, the logarithmic primitive applies only on intervals where the denominator is nonzero. Substituting the endpoints into $\ln|x^{2}-4|$ across this asymptote is invalid. The definite integral is not defined.

foundation.solution_text:
$f(x) = 4+\sin x$, so $f'(x) = \cos x$.
$\int \dfrac{\cos x}{4+\sin x}\,dx$
$= \ln(4+\sin x) + C$

$f(x) = 3-\cos x$, so $f'(x) = \sin x$.
$\int \dfrac{\sin x}{3-\cos x}\,dx$
$= \ln(3-\cos x) + C$

development.question_text: Evaluate $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{\sin x}{2-\cos x}\,dx$ as a single logarithm.
development.solution_text:
$f(x) = 2-\cos x$, so $f'(x) = \sin x$.
$\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{\sin x}{2-\cos x}\,dx$
$= \left[\ln(2-\cos x)\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}$
$= \ln\dfrac{3}{2} - \ln 1$
$= \ln\dfrac{3}{2}$

development.question_text: By writing $\tan x$ as $\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, find $\int \tan x\,dx$.
development.solution_text:
$\int \tan x\,dx$
$= \int \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx$
$f(x) = \cos x$, so $f'(x) = -\sin x$.
$= -\int \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx$
$= -\ln|\cos x| + C$

mastery.question_text: Differentiate $\ln(\ln x)$, and hence find $\int \dfrac{1}{x\ln x}\,dx$ for $x > 1$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\ln x)$
$= \dfrac{1}{\ln x} \times \dfrac{1}{x}$
$= \dfrac{1}{x\ln x}$
The integrand is exactly this derivative.
$\int \dfrac{1}{x\ln x}\,dx = \ln(\ln x) + C$

mastery.question_text: Evaluate $\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \cot x\,dx$, giving an exact answer.

A curve has gradient $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{6x}{3x^{2}+4}$ and passes through $(0,\,5)$.
Find its equation.

mastery.solution_text:
$x^{2}-1 = 0$ when $x = 1$ or $x = -1$.
Both of these lie in the interval from $-1$ to $2$, so the integrand is undefined there.
The rule $\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)| + C$ holds only where $f(x) \ne 0$, so this integral has no value.
